excerpt_original: Bodies carrying life, faces hollowed by time, snow and gravestones. Gary Briechle’s new book, a masterwork of long-unseen pictures, is the most haunted of the autumn. L’article Gary Briechle: “Life makes marks” est apparu en premier sur Blind Magazine .

blocks.text: Gary Briechle’s Maine is nothing like a postcard. Long settled in Rockland, a small working port on the East Coast, the American photographer works in wet plate collodion, a rare and demanding process. For thirty years he has photographed his family, his friends, his neighbors. From each plate he makes a single print, which he gives to his sitter, before the glass is put away in the recesses of his house. His third book, I Want To See A Lighthouse , published by Charcoal Press, finally brings this work out of the dark. Interview.
Your photographs dwell in harsh territory: precariousness, aging, death hovering at the edge of things. Where does this attentiveness to the fragility of existence come from?
Gary Briechle: Our time here is finite. Being here has to mean something. Pressure’s on.

That’s why I stay busy. I shoot. If I see something I want to photograph, I do it right then. I don’t tell myself I’ll come back to it later, because later is a question mark. Every day counts. It’s kind of a pain in the ass, it’s always been hard to relax for me.

I think of life as a line, mostly moving from left to right. It isn’t perfectly straight. And there are loops, stutters, slow and fast. But the direction is clear. Birth is one bookend. Death is the other. In between are the books, the chapters, and the pages—the things we do while we’re here. And on some of those pages are pictures.

I can feel the pressure. I hate myself when I waste a day. But that feeling becomes a powerful motivator for the next day. If I can help it, I never want to let two of those wasted days happen in a row.

My father died at ninety-nine. His mind was still pretty much there. I would look at him and wonder what he had been like as a child. Not in some abstract way—I wanted to see that child inside the old man sitting in front of me. There were photographs in boxes that had been passed down, so I had somewhere to begin. I could look at his face at ninety-nine, then look at a picture of him at five, and feel the connection.
The child and the old man are not opposites. They’re the same life, carried forward. They’re both fragile. They’re both vulnerable. They both need other people. I need help myself, honestly.

Maybe life isn’t a line at all. Maybe it’s a cluster of experiences, events, influences, actions, reactions, things we do, and things done to us. We gather all of it, no sorting. Why bother? We carry it around somehow.
So I shoot. I put things in the box while I can.

There is no denying the relationship between time and photography. The constant flow stops on a dime here and there, and we can look, contemplate, and feel in some saturated rich way, the way movies make us feel or music. Then we start moving again.

blocks.text: Wet plate collodion demands a kind of ceremony: coating the glass, asking your subject to hold still for long seconds. What passes between you and the person you are photographing in that suspended time?

G.B.: There are three characters involved in making a wet plate: the subject, me, and the camera. And really, when I say the camera, I mean the whole process. The big tripod, the big camera, the dark cloth, stuff in the back of the truck. It’s a strange thing to be in front of.

I work in a couple of ways. One is more a set up. But for me, setting something up isn’t any less authentic than street shooting. The subject knows something is happening. They’re participating, and as the photographer, you still have to pick the right moment, except it’s less a decisive moment and more a decisive duration. The picture might need to last a second, or it might need to last thirty seconds. You have to feel where the subject is, along with figuring out the light and all the technical things. But if you’re lucky you get something inward.
I see a lot of blankness, muscleless faces in many portraits. It shows me what not to do. Eyes can be extraordinary and I always pay attention to them.

Because the process is slow—start to finish might take five minutes or so—people tend to settle down a little. They pull out of life for a minute and sit still. A lot of people are hardly ever still. They’re always bouncing around. And stillness is an interesting thing to dip into. With some people I know, being still brings out something marvelous. Something psychologically deep, maybe. I don’t really know how to explain it, but I can see it.

Sometimes I stay behind the camera so they see me there, involved. Other times I move a little to the side and ask them to look at the camera instead of at me. Then it becomes more a picture about them, and less about their relationship with me. They present themselves somehow.

And the big camera brings a seriousness to it. People understand this is involved. They want to help it work out. So these become serious moments, and I like that. I’ve made pictures at birthday parties, and weddings, and I love the fun of that too, but my work generally has a more serious feeling, and the process has something to do with that.

The other way I work, especially when there’s a group of people around, is to say, “Hey, guys, I’m going to put a plate in. If I come up to you, can I ask you to hold still? It’ll only take a minute.” This is particularly funny in a park or some gathering of people. And as long as there’s a few people that will vouch for me, it’s a bit of a game.

I get a manic spike out of this. It’s kind of absurd to think a picture will come out under these circumstances, and I think that’s the attraction. And also I can point to times it worked really well. The goal is always to wind up the day with something I couldn’t have imagined when I started the day. This has gotten me there for sure.
Then I put a plate in without knowing what I’m going to do. I just go out among them and see what happens. Why not?

Mostly those pictures don’t work. I’d say that for sure. But when they do, they can be very alive and complex in a way that a more conventional portrait might not be. There aren’t really any rules to this. I’m trying to bring some of the feeling of working with a small camera into this cumbersome process. Some freedom, some spontaneity.
But the process is always there, participating. It’s the third character making the photograph.

blocks.caption: © Gary Briechle, from I Want To See A Lighthouse, published by Charcoal Press

blocks.text: You spent years as a sculptor before turning to photography. What shifted in the way you saw the world when you moved from matter to light?

G.B.: Yes, sculpture was my focus starting around the age of fifteen, for about twenty years. I liked wood and stone and castings, and I was pretty involved with the surface of objects. Later, I became more interested in the form of things. I still see that distinction in photography.

A really high-resolution digital image can show you so much of the surface of a face. But the form—if you were going to carve that face or make it out of clay—is about the volume of the head, the face itself.

What I love about wet plate is that you can get both on the same plate. You get this intense description, but when someone moves a little during a long exposure, turns a little in space, you can see the form, the sculpture of it. To my eye, collodion has that tendency toward form, partly because of the long exposures.

With sculpture, you make one thing. You might get to a point where you’re done and you like it. Or you might not really like it, but you don’t throw it out. Either way, there’s a point where you move on. And there it is: one thing you made. One sculpture.

I carry some of that into printmaking. I love how glass negatives print, but I usually only want to make one or two prints. I know I could make an edition. For me, though, making an edition feels like a bit of a waste of time. I like the uniqueness of one, maybe two. I usually give a print to the person who sat for me or worked with me, so that’s generally what I do. I’m completely fine with a one-off in photography.
I realize this is a little abstract, but form and surface description are always in play for me, in both sculpture and photography.

And of course sculpture is made with your hands, at least the kind I like. Collodion is very hands-on too. I can’t help thinking that the more involved I am with my hands and my body, the more meaningful the work is to me.
Sometimes a digital picture can feel like it was made by this box I’m holding in front of me, rather than by me.

blocks.caption: © Gary Briechle, from I Want To See A Lighthouse, published by Charcoal Press

blocks.text: In I Want To See A Lighthouse , many of the images show bodies in their most unsparing truth: skin that bears witness to time, flesh worn down by living. What draws you, precisely, to these tired bodies and bruised faces?

G.B.: Let’s compare two hammers. One comes from Home Depot. The other comes from Elmer’s Barn, which is an antiques group shop with a lot of inexpensive things. Not much fancy stuff. I find it a very inspiring place. Almost everything you pick up shows some evidence of somebody’s hands.

Home Depot, well, we all know Home Depot. The hammer has a blue handle, and the steel head and shaft are one piece. The head doesn’t attach to anything. There’s engineering in it. You can feel that somebody figured out how to take that whip of your hand and turn it into the power of the hit. This hammer I have in my shop.

Now, the hammer from Elmer’s I keep in the car has a metal head and a straight wooden handle. The head has this gorgeous patina, the kind of thing only time can make on metal. It’s not rust. There are blues and grays and charcoal colors, and they seem to come from inside the metal rather than sit on the surface.

And the wooden handle is just unbelievably complex. There’s the grain, and there’s oil from hands, or from the shop it lived in. There’s some paint splatter. There are cuts where it looks like the handle got in the path of a saw it shouldn’t have been near. Someone’s initials I can’t make out.

At some point the head got loose, so somebody drove a wedge into the end of the handle to tighten it. Then that must have loosened up, because somebody drove a nail in beside the wedge. Another attempt to keep the head on tight. You can see all of that. Somebody kept using this thing and kept finding ways to make it work.

I don’t think a person can deliberately make a hammer that beautiful. Literally. You could make a beautiful hammer, but you couldn’t put all that time into it. All those little things that happened to it, the complexity of it.

There’s only one of those hammers from Elmer’s Barn in existence. There’s tens of thousands of them from Home Depot. Photography is always about being specific. You try to find something unique and revelatory. That’s the job.

blocks.caption: © Gary Briechle, from I Want To See A Lighthouse, published by Charcoal Press

blocks.text: And that’s something that wet plate can do with a person. It can show skin—a face, an arm, a hand—as something alive with time. You can see life there.

That’s true of a child’s skin too. Time is there in a different way. There’s that smoothness, that almost porcelain quality. Of course, it isn’t the old, weathered hammer. But there’s form and depth, and the light finds it. It shows you something about being alive in that skin.
Life makes marks.
There is a photograph in this book of an infant in a car seat set down in the middle of a cemetery, where birth and death are held in the same frame. What do you seek in this kind of collision?

G.B.: I was with a friend and her baby in a graveyard. Some of the headstones were magnificent. A few had skulls and crossbones carved into them, which is a pretty bizarre thing to come across. Pretty Tim Burton.
I had some silicone molding material to make castings. (And I feel like I should say—the silicone lifted off completely. No residue, no marks, respectful of what was there.)
And the picture just presented itself, like they sometimes do. Nothing very subtle about it. A baby in a graveyard. There were the bookends, right there.
I liked how the plate rendered the whiteness of the baby and the car seat, and depth of field felt right.

I can’t help seeing all of us in a baby. The vulnerability is so clear. With adults, it gets buried under things. We let some of it show, or we find a way to talk about it, but usually pretty sparingly.
But I think it’s still there. We’ve just had more time to cover it up.

There is a quality of deep intimacy in your portraits, as though your subjects were, in some sense, family. What accounts for that closeness, emotional or physical, between you and the people you photograph?
G.B.: The camera is the equal sign between who is in front of it and who is behind it. The energy that passes back and forth is vulnerability and love.
After Gary Briechle in collodion, you made Maine in color, before returning to black and white for this third book. What brought you back to it?

G.B.: Photography has a pretty short history, starting around 1840, give or take, and of course there’s everything that led up to it. I was interested in all of it. I wanted to try everything, and I pretty much did. The mercury involved in daguerreotypes kind of put the kibosh on that one, though.

Pinhole cameras fascinated me. A dark container is about ninety percent of what you need. Coming from sculpture, building cameras was a way into photography. I started making pinhole cameras right away, and I think that gave me a one-at-a-time attitude from the beginning.

It was never really about how much I could shoot in a day. It was about paying attention, picking something out, and being okay with making one or two pictures. More if it happened. And if I didn’t make any, it could still be a good day if I’d done some good looking.

Wet plate seems very complicated on the one hand, but there’s something pretty simple about it, too. There’s a lens, a box, light, and silver that responds to the light. I can still feel the connection to those first pinhole cameras.

blocks.caption: © Gary Briechle, from I Want To See A Lighthouse, published by Charcoal Press

blocks.text: That said, a lot of the time I was doing wet plate, I also had a Leica around my neck. I’d be busy with a plate over by the side of the house, and the kids would be playing on the trampoline, and I’d think, What am I doing over here? The pictures are over there. Sometimes I’d just leave the plate sitting in the camera to dry out and walk over with the Leica. I shot Tri-X in it, of course.

But after years of black-and-white, I got interested in color. Fuji Provia was a particular favorite. It had this plain, quiet color. Velvia could feel like it was shouting at me. Provia didn’t. And it was slide film, so you’d go to the store and get these little pictures back in their mounts. Little spectacular gems. I really liked that. I developed my own C-41 when I used it, but I never got into processing slides.

When the black-and-white book was wrapping up and Jack Woody had pretty much everything he needed, and was developing the sequence, I sent him a couple hundred prints from the Provia pictures. I said, “These aren’t for the book, but maybe they’ll tell you a little more about the people I photograph, or something that doesn’t come across in the black-and-white alone.”
He emailed back and said, “Well, I think this should be your second book.” That was a wow, for sure. I hadn’t expected that.

But things keep changing. Eventually it got harder to find slide processing, and I drifted away from it. I went into digital, and I still carry a digital camera. Sometimes I want all the description I can get. A portrait where you can count the eyelashes. There are times when that feels right to me.

But I’ve mostly come back to collodion, with a little color here and there. Keeping track of the digital work drove me crazy. I had a camera stolen out of the car with a card full of pictures I’d never taken off. Those were just gone.

And even with the pictures I still had, I could never find anything. I’d back things up, put them on different drives, and eventually there was so much stuff that I didn’t really know what I had anymore. Actually, that’s kind of the case with everything with me.
It stopped being fun. And I don’t think there’s any shame in going where the fun is. Or the thing that feels the best.

I don’t want to spend all my time beating myself up about keeping track of things. It’s time I could be making something, or looking at something. Instead I’m fucking around with a program that needs updating, or something that’s stopped working with something else, or a printer that needs six hundred dollars’ worth of ink and also says to me, “I’m sorry, I can no longer work for you until you install a new maintenance cartridge.”
It wore me down. It didn’t feel very human to me.
With collodion, I still like being there, doing it. For me, you just can’t beat that.

blocks.caption: © Gary Briechle, from I Want To See A Lighthouse, published by Charcoal Press

blocks.text: It is said that you store your plates in the attic, under a bed or in a closet; that there is no drive to exhibit, no drive to sell, only to make. What made this book exist?

G.B.: Jesse [Lenz, the founder of Charcoal Press] said he’d like to do a book and that I should send him some stuff to look at. We have known each other for years. Not super well. I’d see him once or twice a year when he came through Rockland. He has always been very enthusiastic and supportive of my work, even before my first two books were published.

Jesse saw me two years ago at a coffee shop I go to often and told me he was finally ready to do the “Definitive Gary Briechle” book. This coincided with me being at a certain stage and having all the stuff around the house, practically all of it has never been seen, and it’s started to feel like a bit of a bummer, so I thought this would be great, to do this book at this point, to get some of these things out in the world.
I really like the people I photograph. There’s a lot of people I know really well, literally for over 20 years, and I knew they would get a kick out of seeing themselves in a book.

A big obstacle for me is trying to talk about my work. Not a whole lot to talk about in a way. I think things can exist purely visually and that could be that. And I’m not much of a networker. I like left field where you watch the game more than you play it.

Everyone I take a portrait of, I make a print for the person who is in it. Those are like little micro exhibits. The person sees themselves, their girlfriend sees them, their mom and dad and some friends might see them. So in a way I’ve had a whole hell of a lot of micro exhibits over the last 30 years, and that feels so awesome, to give people pictures.

I think exhibiting once in a while feels good. You’re able to say to your mom and dad, “Hey, look, I’m not completely nuts.” But I think the networking, smooshing, inflated art talking about work feels not as good as doing the work.

And to me, the book is the ultimate exhibit. So I feel very happy and fortunate that Jesse is doing the book. And it’s a BIG book. If I can, I have a book going every 8 to 10 years or so, and that’s plenty.

blocks.caption: © Gary Briechle, from I Want To See A Lighthouse, published by Charcoal Press

blocks.text: It’s funny. The boxes of glass plates are extremely heavy. Often 80 or 90 5×7 plates in a small box, usually wooden, standing vertically. It never feels right to put them all on one series of shelves or in one place. They’re just too freaking heavy, so I put them all over the house. Kind of spreading the weight around.

Pulling things out for Jesse kind of drove me nuts because I’m like a stranger to my own work and I don’t know where it is. I don’t know what’s in the boxes. It’s frustrating, but it was also kind of fun. Like, oh yeah, I remember that one. Jesse said he liked that we were both seeing images for the first time together.
I guess I do what I wanna do. It’s a preference. It’s not much of a choice between things like networking, talking, doing gallery stuff and actually doing the work.
I guess I just like to actually do the work. I really really like to do the work. It’s a way of life.
No lighthouse appears anywhere in this book, and yet the title stands: I Want To See A Lighthouse , drawn from a child’s wish. Why this title, for these images?

G.B.: With photography, you have a relationship with the world. You’re not on your own. You’re responding to what’s around you. It begins with recognition: there is something here worth looking at, worth taking time to consider.

Years ago, I found a child’s notebook on the floor of the dump store in Rockland. That’s where people leave things they think someone else might want, and other people come to see what they can use. I don’t know whose notebook it was. On one page were the words, “I want to see a lighthouse.” And it was part of a hangman game.

Maine has a rocky coast, often hidden in fog. There are lighthouses everywhere. We’ve come to think of them as decorations—pictures on calendars and coffee mugs. It’s easy to forget what they were there for. Someone out on the water, in danger, needed to see a light. They needed a path into a safe harbor.
I think we all need that now. Sometimes it feels as though the whole world does. The stakes are really high.

But the sentence in the notebook was part of a game of hangman. In the upper left corner, you can see the little figure, partly drawn. That changes the words for me. There is still a chance to find the lighthouse, but there aren’t many guesses left. You need to find it while there’s still time. And this is by a child. A child wants to find a lighthouse. What does this say about the anxiety we instill in our children?

When you turn the page, there’s another sheet of ruled paper, shaded with dark pencil. The black is closing in around the white. I don’t know what the child intended, or whether the two pages had anything to do with each other. But I can’t help seeing them together.
To me, they carry the same feeling: there is still light, and only so much time to find it.

blocks.caption: © Gary Briechle, from I Want To See A Lighthouse, published by Charcoal Press

blocks.text: Your work has sometimes been set alongside that of Ralph Eugene Meatyard, for its sense of the uncanny, or Diane Arbus, for the frontality of her gaze and her recurring twins. I would add Roger Ballen, for the childlike drawings, the bones, the dark black-and-white world. Are there artists, be they photographers, painters or writers, whose work in particular inspires you?

G.B.: Diane Arbus is the big one for me. I’m very familiar with her monograph, the Revelations book and the book Untitled . I like her writings in the Revelations book. You could see the mania in the way she wrote a list. I relate to that. Her quotes in the monograph are some of the best words ever written about photography in my opinion. She is the quintessential example of what being “all in” means.

When I first saw her work, I didn’t get it in terms of how she made this picture. But over time I have developed a visual for it: she’s on a train going somewhere by herself. There is a train running parallel to her filled with people. For some reason very, very briefly the trains stop on the platform, both doors open and she sees into it, to the people. Really only for a blink of an eye. Then the door is closed and the trains move on. I have the sense of a wink or a blink, but she’s there with her camera and she has access to this parallel world. I remember thinking, “I want to see that world,” and I had no idea how to do it.

Over time I got a couple glimpses into it. It’s still a mystery, but I know it can happen. Most of what I make is crap, like beyond embarrassing crap, let’s put it at 98%. But I do get moments of the doors opening. That’s all you need.

There is a purity about Arbus. I really admire her. I know truth is a word that is maligned in photography. It’s like a joke, it’s so obvious that photography is not truthful. I guess, like, if you said on a test at Yale, “Diane Arbus tells the truth,” it would drag your score down a bit, but unquestionably for me there’s a personal and psychological truth in her work that’s beyond criticism.

Disfarmer is outwardly so plain, but unparalleled sensitivity. I like Eggleston a ton, he’s quirky. Well seen images. He is the definition of all in. Mark Cohen, what he does on the street is so affecting. Seems like the doors on the train open for him a lot.
I Want To See A Lighthouse by Gary Briechle is published by Charcoal Press , 2026. Hardcover, linen with a tipped-in image, 224 pages, 11 × 14 inches, $85.
